user_direction: Continue with John as the actor. Move the bed near the back fence, show less of the shed, favour the digging action and show turf already removed and piled beside the bed.
prompt:
Redo the first reference, the three photographic illustrations of John double-digging, in a markedly new closely framed camera shot. A wide 3:1 triptych of three equal square natural colour photographs, minimal thin white vertical seams. No letters, explanation, numerals or captions. British vegetable-growing book, small page 160 pictures. Priority is correct preparation, intelligible action, and down-to-earth realism. Ref 2 is the real John's face and clothing, same man in three photos, sleeves rolled, worn jeans and practical muddy boots. Ref 3 is the true home garden layout, aerial as a map ONLY. Ref 4 shows the thin root-bound layers of turf stacked upside down, this is a texture and technique reference only. The illustration must look fully photographic.
NEW LOCATION AND FRAMING: Move the new bed to the FAR/BACK section of the home lawn where the greenhouses have been removed, near the grey boundary fence just RIGHT of the real blue shed; former bed frames/greenhouses gone. Keep the stepping-stone path in its actual position, now toward the photographer and OUTSIDE the tight crop. Use a gardener's close over-the-shoulder-to-side view with the camera looking down at a strong angle from slightly above John's hands, almost all frame is earth and tool action. In EACH square at least three quarters of the picture is the work area with stripped bed, cross-trench, stack, hands and tool. Narrow distant glimpse of blue-painted horizontal shed boards clips just the very upper-left corner, 3-6 percent of picture, perhaps a little weathered fence along the top. Do NOT show a whole shed/door, house, skyline, paving stripe, extensive grass, old beds or structures. Allow John's upper body or head to crop at top and side; his checked workshirt, receding hair and short beard when visible identify him. Prefer authentic working posture with weight through the tool and strong variations in pose to three portraits of the same pose. Maintain same bed, background and lens across sequence, movements credible.
CRUCIAL CORRECTION TO EVERY PANEL — the ENTIRE rectangular footprint of this future vegetable bed has already had the lawn turf sliced off, all the way from the near end to the far end. All of this footprint beyond the trench is bare, level, relatively firm earth with a little scattered dark compost, visibly different from newly overturned soil. A narrow border of living grass ONLY OUTSIDE the footprint. Readable straight perimeter between uncut grass and low stripped brown soil. Actual trench cuts into BARE EARTH, not sod. At the left side of the bed IN ALL THREE FRAMES show a single conspicuous modest, irregular layered stack of several thin manageable rectangular freshly cut grass turves OUTSIDE the bed. Soil/root sides face UP, cut grass sides DOWN; thin blades and matted roots fringe each seam. A practical pile of real sod pieces loosely squared with slightly uneven or curled corners, not bricks, uniform tiles or loose compost. Pile uncovered because work is underway. Keep it clearly distinct from a small heap of loose excavated brown TOPSOIL reserved just beside the far end of the bed for final refilling. Show that reserved heap separately where visible. Neither pile blocks the action. 
THREE INSTANTS of work oriented looking up the bed from its near edge, all tools level contact with a realistic adult, moderate-sized bed, shallow full-width trench across short axis one spade blade (~25 cm) deep and one blade wide front-to-back. Composition reads clearly even at 43 mm square in print:
LEFT. Open the first trench across the near end of the STRIPPED bed. John at the side of the cut in three-quarter profile and bent knees with both hands in different places on the same short adult garden spade. Caught mid-lift, modest load of bare topsoil emerging from first trench, being saved. See the cut face and flat exposed trench floor. The separate leafy-edged pile of cut turves is plainly visible left of work.
CENTRE. SAME opening still empty of topsoil. John levers the lower soil in place using a strong FOUR-TINE gardening fork; ONE boot on firm ground on right, one boot can be on the fork shoulder down in the excavation. Show a different posture putting weight DOWN. Steel fork shoulder down inside the open trench, four tines plunged DEEPLY into the actual trench FLOOR and mostly buried, only the very tops of tines visible. Handle inclined to lever crumbly lower clods with a little dark compost. The action is penetrating below the first spade depth, do not show four shiny full-length prongs resting ON TOP or a gardener lifting forkful from hole. 
RIGHT. Previous near strip has been partly backfilled with distinctly rough loose topsoil; OPEN second parallel trench immediately BEHIND it recedes by just a single spade width into that BARE unturfed ground. From the side John directs a spadeful into the first trench, medium-sized irregular clods falling in a short trajectory onto the loose front strip, the adjacent working gap visible, separate reserved pile and sod stack undisturbed. 
Ground perspective, clothes and tools credible in scale, leave narrow workable edges and a view into the soil. Organic minor variations between exposures, natural Cornish daylight, readable soil texture, natural contrast, real garden photography, no cutaway graphics, no floating soil block. Prioritise brown stripped bed over surroundings in all three pictures.
